7.1. Rulers of Mughal Empire :
The great Mughal Empire history in India spans from 1526 (Christian Era) to 1857
C.E. The Mughals established a firm foundation in administration, a solid economy and
flourishing trade. Babur established Mughal empire after defeating Ibrahim Lodi the last
ruler of Delhi sultanate at Panipat in 1526 C.E. It marked the beginning of Mughal empire.
The empire extended from Bengal in the East to Afghanistan in the West and from
Himalayas in the North to Golkonda in the South.

Map-7.1 Mughal Empire during Akbar’s Period
Babur (1526-1530 C.E.) :
Babur was the founder of the Mughal empire. He
was a great genius at devising war tactics. He also conquered
Delhi and Agra after the first battle of Panipat. He was one
of the greatest poet in Turkish literature, and Nature lover.
Babur died in 1530 C.E.

Analyze the reasons why the Mughal empire was first
established in northern India.

Fig-7.2 Babur

Babur was related to Timur from his father’s side and to Genghis Khan's dynasty
from his mother's side. The Mughals (descendants of Mongols) preferred to call
themselves the Chaghatayids, after Genghis Khan's second son, Chaghatay.

The Word “Mughal” comes from “Mongol”.

Humayun (1530-1540 & 1555-1556 C.E.) :
Humayun was the second Mughal ruler. He was the son
and successor of Babur. He was inexperienced at the time of
ascending to the throne and faced bitter rivalry from his brothers.
Sher Shah Suri was consolidating his power in Bihar and Bengal
and was emerging as a powerful ruler. Sher shah defeated
Humayun at Chausa in 1539 C.E. and Kanauj in 1540 C.E. and
forced him to flee to Iran. In Iran, Humayun received help from
Safavid Shah and recaptured Delhi in 1555 C.E. He died in
1556 C.E.

Fig-7.3: Humayun

Sher Shah (1540-1545 C.E.) :

Sher Shah Suri was an Afghan leader who had
progressed on his own. He defeated Humayun twice
and therefore established the Sur Dynasty in Delhi.
After gaining control over Delhi, he won many other
important battles. He then extended his Empire from
Kabul to Bengal and Malwa.
He was not only a great warrior but also an
administrator. During his five years reign he
introduced many reforms i.e. created a land revenue
system, introduced new currency, provided a postal
service etc., He died in 1545 C.E. due to artillery
explosion.

Fig-7.4: Sher Shah

Humayun captured Delhi in 1555 C.E. due to the
inefficiencies of Sher Shah's successors.

Akbar (1556-1605 C.E.) :
Akbar was just 13 years old when his father Humayun
passed away. Since Akbar was very young, his guardian
Bhairam Khan took care of the administration on behalf of
Akbar. Hemu, the prime minister of Bengal wanted to capture
Delhi. Hemu was defeated and killed at the second battle of
Panipat by Akbar in 1556 C.E. Akbar consolidated his rule
strongly in Delhi and Agra. He annexed Chunar and Malwa.
Akbar annexed the Rajput state of Gondwana. Later, he
conquered some territories like Bikaner, Jaisalmer and Jodhpur.

Fig-7.5: Akbar

Akbar followed cordial relations towards the Rajputs who were honest and brave. He
married Jodhabai, the princess of Jaipur. Akbar appointed the Rajputs in higher positions.
Raja Mansingh, Raja Todarmal, Raja Bhagavan Das were the notable ones. Mewad ruler
Maha Rana Pratap fought with Akbar throughout his life.

What would have happened in the Mughal Empire if there was no Bhairam

Jahangir (1605-1627 C.E.) :
Salim the successor of Akbar came to the throne with the
title Jahangir (world conqueror). He continued his father’s
traditions. He expanded his kingdom by establishing good relations
with the Rajputs. He imposed local trade, and commercial taxes
to strengthen his kingdom financially. He was able to take a close
look at birds, plants, animals and tell them about their value. He
mainly loved birds. He was also a great painter. His wife Nurjahan
took over the administration when he was ill during the last
period of his rule.

Fig-7.6: Jahangir

Shah Jahan (1628-1658 C.E.) :
Shah Jahan was the son of Jahangir, also called Khurram. Under
his reign the Mughal Empire reached the peak of its cultural glory.
Best remembered for the grand monuments constructed during his
reign, especially the Taj Mahal, the Moti Masjid (Pearl mosque) in
Agra, the Jami Masjid and Red Fort in Delhi. During his reign he also
conquered the Deccan Kingdoms of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and
Golkonda. In 1658 C.E., there was a conflict over succession among
Fig-7.7: Shah Jahan
Shah Jahan’s sons and finally Aurangzeb ascended the throne.
Aurangzeb (1658 -1707 C.E.) :
He was the younger son of Shah Jahan. He was a devout Muslim
and led his life as per the principles of Quran. It is said that even if
he was the emperor of India, he would cover his own expenses
(including food and clothing) with the money he earned by sewing
hats. He did not show tolerance to other religions. He faced a large
number of revolts all over his kingdom i.e. Assam, Rajasthan, Punjab,
Deccan, etc., Guru Tejh Bahadur, Guru Govind Singh, Shivaji revolted
against him. Among them Shivaji succeeded in establishing an
independent Maratha kingdom. After the death of Shivaji, Aurangzeb
invaded Deccan. Aurangzeb conquered Bijapur in 1685 C.E. and
Golkonda in 1687 C.E. His death was followed by inheritance struggle
amongst his sons.

7.2. Political, Social & Economic life :
7.2.1. Administration :
The Mughals had a centralized administration. All power vested with the emperor.
A council of ministers assisted him in administration. Babur and Humayun had less impact
on administration, as they did not rule for a long period.
Akbar introduced a number of administrative reforms. He divided his vast empire into
several “Subas” and appointed a “Subedar” for each suba. A “Suba” was the term for a
province in the Mughal Empire. Akbar divided his kingdom into 15 Subas. Subas were
divided into “Sarkars”. These Sarkars were divided into “Paraganas”. The same pattern was
followed by all other Mughal emperors.
Akbar surveyed the land and introduced the agrarian method of determining tax
according to the crop. The land was divided into four types and one-third of the crop was
collected as tax. Impressions of Sher Shah’s administration could be noticed to some extent
in Akbar’s rule.

Mansabdari System :
Akbar introduced the Mansabdari
system in his military policy. The term
mansabdar refers to an individual who
holds a mansab, meaning a position
or rank. It was a grading system used
by the Mughals to fix Rank, Salary and
Military responsibilities. Each
mansabdar consisted of 10 to 10,000
soldiers.

Fig-7.9:
A Mansabdar on march with his sawars

Relations of Mughals with other rulers :
The Mughals campaigned and fought against rulers who did not obey them. As a part
of their diplomacy, Mughals maintained relations with Rajputs by marrying their daughters,
offering better position in their court. The Sisodiyas did not accept Mughal authority. The
good relations with Rajputs, Sikhs and other rulers during Akbar's time began to
deteriorate during Shajahan's time and became worse during the reign of Aurangzeb. There
were revolts in all parts of the empire during his reign. The empire declined very quickly
after the death of Aurangzeb.

7.2.2. Social Life :
Religion :
Mughals are Sunni Muslims. Among them Akbar showed religious tolerance.
He abolished “Jizya tax” and “Pilgrim tax” levied on the Hindus. Akbar allowed religious
ceremonies of people to be celebrated openly. The majority of the people in the society
were Hindus. The society in those days consist of not only Hindus and Muslims but also
of the Buddhists, the Jains, the Sikhs and the Parsis. Aurangzeb also appointed clergymen
named Mutawasibs to observe the moral life of the people as per Sharia or Islamic principles.
Jizya Tax :
The Jizya tax is a tax paid by non-Muslims to Muslim rulers for practicing their
religion and obtaining exemptions from joining the Army. This tax was first introduced
by Qutb-ud-din aibak, the founder of the slave dynasty.
Pilgrim Tax :
A tax imposed on hindus by the muslim emperors for under taking a journey to
a religious or sacred place.

Akbar, in 1575 C.E. built a meeting house of
worship called Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri.
In 1582 C.E. He proclaimed a new religion called
Din-I-Ilahi. Literally meaning “Peace with all”,
Universal Peace or absolute peace. As applied by
Akbar, it described a peaceful and harmonious
relationship among different religions. Only 18
people joined this religion. This remained a court
religion.

Fig-7.10: Ibadat Khana

7.2.3. Economic Life :
The Indian Economy prospered under the Mughal Empire. Agriculture and trade also
progressed. Agriculture was the main occupation of the people.
The Mughals were responsible for building an extensive road system, creation of uniform
currency, and the unification of the country. The Empire had an extensive road network
built by a public works department set up by the Mughals. It designed, constructed and
maintained roads, linking towns and cities across the empire. This was one of the reasons
for the expansion of trade. The important source of income was the revenue from agricultural
tax.

Discuss with your teacher the method of levying agricultural tax during the
Mughal period.
Coinage :
The Mughals adopted
and standardized the Rupee
(silver) and Dam (copper)
currencies introduced by the
Sur emperor Sher shah Sur
during his brief rule. The
Dam was initially the most
common coin in Akbar’s
time.

Fig-7.11: Coins

Agriculture :
Indian Agricultural production increased under the Mughal Empire. A variety of crops
were grown, including food crops such as wheat, rice, and barley and cash crops such as
cotton, opium and indigo. Indian cultivators began to grow extensively the commercial
crops Maize and Tobacco.
Zabt :
A remarkable feature of the Mughal system under Akbar was his revenue administration,
developed largely under the supervision of his famed revenue minister Raja Todar Mal. It
took two decades for Akbar to develop and implement a revenue system that would benefit
both the State and the Farmers. In 1580 C.E. he obtained the previous 10 years’ local
revenue statistics, detailed productivity and price fluctuations, and averaged the produce of
different crops and their prices. It ranged from one-third to one-half of production value
and was payable in “dams”. This system was called zabt.

Compare the present land revenue system to that of Mughal system.

7.3. Art & Architecture :
A new tradition of architecture was started during the Mughal era. The monuments
were constructed on high plinths. Marble was mostly used as construction material and
constructed water flowing fountains extensively. Besides marble, coloured (precious and
semi-precious) stones were used to decorate the buildings.
Fatehpur Sikri :
After his military victories over Chittor and Ranthambore, Akbar decided to shift his
capital from Agra to a new location, on the Sikri ridge, to honor the Sufi saint Sheikh Salim
Chishti. Here he commenced the construction of a planned walled city. He named the city,
Fatehbad, with Fateh, meaning 'victorious' which was later called Fatehpur Sikri. Fatehpur
Sikri is one of the best-preserved collections of Mughal architecture in India.
Buland Darwaza :
Buland Darwaza or the lofty gate was built by the
great Mughal emperor, Akbar at Fatehpur Sikri. Akbar
built the Buland Darwaza, as a “victory arch” to
commemorate his successful Gujarat campaign. Panch
Mahal is another notable five storeyed building in Fatehpur
Sikri with excellent architectural design.

Fig-7.12: Buland Darwaza

Red Fort :
The Red Fort was built as the
fortified family palace of Shahjahanabad,
capital of the Mughal Emperor Shah
Jahan. The Red Fort is considered to
represent the zenith of Mughal creativity
under Shah Jahan and consists of other
important structures such as the Diwane-Aam, Diwan-e-Khas, Moti Masjid,
Hayat Bakhsh Bagh and Rang Mahal.
Fig-7.13: Red Fort

The Taj Mahal :
The Taj Mahal is a white marble
mausoleum located in Agra, Uttar
Pradesh, India. It was built by Mughal
Emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his
wife, Mumtaz. Taj Mahal is regarded as
the finest example of the Mughal
architecture and is considered as one of
the Seven Wonders of the World. The
Taj Mahal is widely recognized as ‘The
jewel of Mughal art in India and one of
the universally admired masterpieces of
the world’s heritage’.

Fig-7.14: Taj Mahal

Culture :
The Mughal Empire was definitive in the early-modern and modern period of Indian
history, with its legacy in India seen in cultural contributions such as,

The combination of Persian art and literature with Indian art.

The development of Mughal clothing, jewellery and fashion, utilizing richly decorated
fabrics such as muslin silk, brocade and velvet.

The evolution and refinement of Mughal and Indian architecture.

The construction of Maktab schools, where youth were taught the Quran and
Islamic law such as the Fatwa-i-Alamgir in their indigenous languages.

Literature :
Persian language was the dominant and official
language of the Empire. Babur nama was written by Babur.
Abul Fazal was a great scholar during the period of Akbar's
regime. He wrote Ain-I-Akbari and Akbar Nama, TuzukI-Jahangiri or jahangir nama was an autobiography of
Jahangir. It was writen by jahangir. Shajahan’s son Dara Fig-7.15: Akbar receiving the
Shikoh translated the Bhagavat Gita, Mahabharata into Akbar Nama from Abul Fazal
Persian language. The most influential Hindi poet Tulsidas wrote the Hindi version of the
Ramayana, the Ramacharithmanas.
Painting :
A new school of art known as miniature painting emerged
during the Mughal period. The art of painting reached its peak
under the patronage of Jahangir Mughal paintings. The colours
peacock blue, Indian red were newly introduced in mughal
paintings.
Music :
Though Babar and Humayun also encouraged music, but it
reached their height during Akbar’s era. According to Abul
Fazal, there were 36 singers in Akbar’s court. The most famous
among them was Tansen and Bajbahadur. Akbar himself used
to play Nakara (Nagara) well. Tansen was one of Akbar’s
navratnas. It is said that he could work miracles with his singing.
Occasionally he could create rain by singing the Megh Malhar,
fire by singing rag Dipak. The present Hindustani Music have
the references of these styles.

End of Mughal Rule :

The decline of Mughal empire started with Shah jahan and ended with Aurangzeb.
The Mughal empire declined quickly after the death of Aurangzeb. The following are the
reasons for the decline:

The suspicious nature and policies of Aurangzeb did not allow any of his sons or
nobles to grow to be capable. His religious bigotry resulted in the revolts of Jats,
Satnamis, and Sikhs. His rivalry with Rajputs and Marathas brought misfortune
for his empire.

The heirs of Aurangzeb proved incapable. Most of them have been addicted to
luxurious life.
Most of the nobles had become corrupt.
The wars of succession for the empire among the sons weakened the administration.
The Deccan policy of Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb further weakened the empire.
Invasions of Ahmad Shah, Nadir Shah and the revolts of Mansabdars also caused
the downfall.
The Mughal Empire, founded by Babur in 1526 C.E, collapsed in 1857 C.E, during
the reign of Bahadur Shah-II.

7.4. Contemporary Kingdom :

The contemporary rulers during Mughals were Afghans, Rajputs, Marathas, and Bahaman
kings. They opposed Mughal rulers and fought with them. In course of time most of these
rulers could not completely succeed in defeating the Mughals. But the Maratha ruler Shivaji
could resist the expansion of Mughals and established an independent kingdom.
Shivaji - Maratha Kingdom (1674 - 1680 CE) :
Marathas were the ones who fought relentlessly against the Mughals in the Deccan
region, when Mughals were at their height of power in North India. Shivaji was the founder
of the Maratha kingdom.
Shivaji was born in Shivaneri fort near Pune. His father was Shaji Bhonsle. He held
a high post in the office of the Sultan of Bijapur. Shivaji was brought up under the care of
his mother Jijabai. He was inspired by the teachings of Samartha Ramadas and other
Maratha saints. His tutor Dadaji Khondadev and Tanaji Malasure taught him the lessons
of warfare. Shivaji assembled the Maratha leaders and Mavalis, the tribal people of Western
Ghats and built a strong brigade.
Extension of Kingdom :
At the age of 19, Shivaji captured Torana Durga,
which was under the control of Muhammad Adilshah
of Bijapur. After this, he won Raigarh, Simhagarh,
Pratapgarh etc., one by one. Enraged by this the Sultan
of Bijapur sent his general Afzal Khan to suppress
Shivaji. Afzal Khan wanted to kill Shivaji deceitfully.
So he invited Shivaji under the pretext of
reconciliation. Expecting this, Shivaji killed Afzal Khan
with ‘Vyaghra Nakha’ (Tiger’s claw), a weapon that he
had with him.
On learning these advancements of Shivaji,
Aurangzeb sent his general Shaista Khan to Deccan
province to curb him down. But clever Shivaji was
able to defeat Shaista Khan.

8.1. Bhakti Movement :
If we look at the course of human history, humans have been using air, water, soil
and fire for his needs since the time of primitive man. He realized that he could live only
through these. Behind these laws of nature, he believed that there was some mighty power.
He thought it was God. Each time they also had to deal with the dangers they posed. He
thus developed a sense of respect, fear, and reverence for these forces of nature. Gradually
this feeling was transformed into devotion. Over time came the concept of devotion along
with human civilization.
Medieval period has underwent a lot of transformation because of the existing
socio economic conditions in the society and also due to the foreign invasions. The society
was fragmented into castes and there were caste distinctions in the society. There has been
constant threat from the foreign rulers.
There was a lot of despair and disunity in the society people were losing confidence
in themselves. At that time saints from different parts of the country tried to bring about
a reform in the society. They moved from across the country and preached society about
equality, brotherhood, unity etc., They devoted their lives for bringing about harmony
among different religions and sections of the society. This movement has spread over a
period of many centuries and one such movement is Bhakti movement.

The Bhakti movement started in 8th century and continued up to 17th century. This
movement spread all over India. Reformers in all religions said that evil practices and, blind
faiths lead them to reform their religions. The reformers adopted singing hymns and
praises to God in their own languages and made compositions. People from all walks of life
became their disciples. They brought about a lot of reform in the society. They preached
people irrespective of their caste, creed, religion etc.
What is Bhakti?
Bhakti means devotion to God. It means attachment, a state of mind where the
devotee surrenders himself or herself unquestioningly. It is building a strong relation between
the devotee and God.
It has the characteristics like universal brotherhood and equality of all in the society
in Hinduism there are different paths of attaining moksha or Godhood. They are karma,
Gnana, Bhakti etc. During the medieval period the path of Bhakti became more popular in
all religions.

The two types of bhakti are Saguna Bhakti and Nirguna Bhakti. Saguna Bhakti means
worshiping God with form, Nirguna Bhakti means worshiping God without form.
Journey of the Bhakti movement :
The movement was started by Adi Shankaracharya. He preached the Adwaitha
philosophy and Madhwacharya had preached Dwaitha Philosophy and Ramanujacharya
preached visishtaadwaitha. Alwars were Vaishnava saints, Nayanars were Saiva saints. They
came from all castes. They spread the Bhakti movement in south India, mainly in Tamil
Nadu.
Later the movement was taken forward by Basaveswara in Karnataka, Tukaram,
Nam dev, Samardha Ramadas etc in Maharastra, Ramananda, Kabir, Ravidas, Surdas, Mirabai
etc in North India; Chaitanya Mahaprabhu in Bengal; Guru Nanak dev in Punjab, and
Shankaradev
Assam. and Atman are different entities
Dwaitha -inBrahman
Vishishtaadwaitha - Individual soul is part of the entity
Adwaitha - Each soul is Divine
Main features of the Bhakti Movement :
1. Oneness of God.
2. One of the ways to moksha is Bhakthi.
3. Bhakthi means surrender to God.
4. Emphasized equality of all humans.
5. No discrimination of caste, creed, section etc.,
6. The bhakti saints travelled to various places to speak about the path of Bhakti and
preached in the local languages.

Sankaracharya was born in Kaladi of Kerala. He became a
saint at the age of five. He preached the Adwaitha Philosophy. He
established four Shakti Peethas in all the four corners of India i.e
Badri in the North, Srungeri in the South, Puri in the East and
Dwaraka in the west. He Wrote Viveka chudamani,
Soundaryalahari, Sivanandalahari, Atmabodha etc. He attained
nirvana at the age of 32. He was considered the greatest reformer

Ramanujacharya :
Ramanujacharya was a philosopher and social reformer. He
was born at Sri Perumbudur in Southern India in the year 1017
C.E. Ramanuja gave a philosophical basis to the teachings of
Vaishnavism. He preached the Visishtaadwaitha. He stated that
everyone could attain salvation by completely surrendering to
the will of the Almighty. He wrote a commentary on the Brahma
Sutras popularly known as "Sri Bhasya".
Fig-8.3: Ramanujacharya

Madhwacharya :
Madhwacharya was born on the west coast of Karnataka
state in 13th century. He preached the Dwaitha philosophy.
Dwaitha - means duality, dualism. It considers Brahman and
Atman as two different entities and Bhakti (devotion) is the
route to eternal salvation. According to Dwaita philosophy
the world is not an illusion but a reality. Brahman, Atman and
matter are unique in nature.

Fig-8.4: Madhwacharya

Vallabhacharya :
Vallabhacharya was another prominent Vaishnava saint
from the South. He hailed from a Telugu family. He gained great
popularity for his talent, scholarship and deep knowledge of
philosophy. His idealogy is known as Suddhadvaita (pure NonDualism). According to it God is one. Vallabhas teachings are also
known as Pushtimarga or the Path of Grace. He had intense love
for the divine incarnation of Lord Shri Krishna. He wrote Fig-8.5: Vallabhacharya
commentaries on the Brahma Sutra.

The Brahma Suthras is a Sanskrit text, attributed to the sage Badarayana or
Vyasa. It is also known as Vedanta Sutra.

Basaveswara :
Basaveswara was a statesman, philosopher, poet, and social
reformer of Karnataka. He popularised Veerasaivism. His literary
works are named Vachanas. He preached to all people irrespective
of his birth or social status. His famous quote is "All men are equal.
There is no caste or sub-caste".

Fig-8.6: Basaveswara

Ramananda :
The credit for the spread of Vaishnava religion in northern
India goes to Ramananda. He was born at Prayag. He got his schooling
in Banaras. He visited various religious places in northern India, and
he preached Vaishnavism. He believed in Vishistadvaita philosophy
of Ramanuja and carried his teachings much further. He strongly
opposed sectarianism. He adopted Hindi to spread his teachings. Fig-8.7: Ramananda

Why did Ramananda oppose sectarianism? Know from your teacher.

Kabir :
Another prominent saint of the Bhakti movement in
northern India was Kabir. He was brought up by a Muslim
weaver named Niru. From his childhood itself Kabir was a
meditative child. When he grew young, he became the disciple
of Ramananda and stayed most of the time at Banaras. He
learnt the Vedanta philosophy in a modified and more acceptable
way from Ramananda. He preached a religion of love which
aimed at promoting unity amongst all castes and creeds. He
advocated “All are equal before God”. In fact, he was the first
saint who tried to reconcile Hinduism and Islam.

Fig-8.8: Kabir

Kabir said that “All are equal before God”? Do you agree with this statement?
Mention your reasons.

Sant Ravidas :
Sant Ravidas lived at Banaras. He lived a life of simplicity and
contentment. There is a spirit of harmony in his writings. He
advocated complete surrender to God. His cardial quote was "Hari
is in all and all in Hari".
Fig-8.9: Ravidas

Mira Bai :
Mira Bai was another important woman saint of the medieval
times. Mira became a devotee of Krishna right from her childhood.
Even after marriage she continued her devotion towards Krishna
and became popular as a Divine singer. Mira lived a very simple
life though she was born in a royal family. She propagated Krishna
Bhakthi among all sections of the society.
Hermits of various religions visited Chittor (Rajastan) to listen
to her Singing in ecstasy. She was the disciple of Sant Ravidas. Her
songs have become popular for centuries.

Fig-8.10: Mira Bai

Chaitanya Mahaprabhu :
He is also known as Sri Gauranga. He was a popular Vaishnava
saint and reformer from Bengal. He visited various religious places
located in the southern and western parts of the country like
Pandharpur, Somnath, Dwarka etc., and preached his teachings
there. He also paid a pilgrimage to Brindavan, Mathura and other
places in the north. However, he finally settled down at Puri and
stayed there till his last breathe. Chaitanya believed in one Supreme
being, whom he called Krishna or Hari. Chaitanya preached that
the presence of the God could be realised through love, devotion,
song and dance. He gave importance to the esoteric way of realisation,
which he believed could be attained through a guru alone.

Mahaprabhu

Shankara deva :
Shankara deva is the saint of Assam. He was a poet, play writer
and social reformer. He founded many Satras or monasteries and
Nam-Ghars in which people of all castes meet for religious and
social purposes. Sankaradeva succeeded in preaching Vaishnavism
among all people including tribal people.
Fig-8.12: Shankara deva
Guru Nanak :
Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh religion was another
prominent saint. He greatly appreciated the teachings of Kabir.
Guru Nanak was born at the village Talwandi near Lahore in 1469.
Right from his childhood he took delight in religious discussions
with holy men. He believed in truth, fraternity of men, righteous
living, the social virtues of dignity of labour and charity.

Fig-8.13: Guru Nanak

He believed in the oneness of God and the brotherhood of men. Nanak preached
in the language of the people and his preachings became very popular during his lifetime
itself. His disciples included both the Hindus and the Muslims. His followers were known
as Sikhs.
The most famous teachings attributed to Guru Nanak are that there is only one god,
and that all human beings can have direct access to God. His most progressive social teachings
denounced the caste system and taught that everyone is equal, regardless of caste and gender.

8.2.Sufi Movement :
The Sufi movement was a socio-religious movement in Islam. The Sufis emphasised on
an egalitarian society based on universal love. The word Sufi is derived from an Arabic word
Saf. Saf means purity / clean. The Sufi saints were always in meditation and they led a
simple life.
The salient features of Sufism :
There is only one God. All are children of God.
To love a fellow human being is to love God.
Devotional music is one of the ways to reach the presence of God.
Sufi believes Wahdat-ul-Wujud which means worship for a single God.
Khwaja Moinuddin Chisti :
Khwaja Mouinuddin Chishti was a great
Sufi Saint of India. The Chishti order was
established in India by him. He was born in
1143 A.D. in Seistan in Persia. He came to
India around 1192 A.D. He spread the message
of love and universal brotherhood.
Fig-8.18: Moinuddin Chishti Darga
Moinuddin Chishti Dargah is located at Ajmer, Rajasthan in India. The shrine
has the grave of the revered saint, Moinnuddin Chishti.
Nizam-ud-din Auliya (1235-1325)
Nizam-ud-din Auliya was the most famous of the chisti Saints. He was the disciple
of Baba Farid. He laid much emphasis on love which leads one to the realization of God.
He also said that love of God means love of humanity. Thus he spread the message of
universal love and brotherhood.
Farid-ud-din Ganj-i-Shakar, Shaik Nizamtullah and Khwaja-pir-mohammad are other

9.1. Brief background of the Indian Constitution :
Students, you know very well that before independence, our India was ruled by the
British. Can you say there was any Constitution for India during the British rule? No, there
was no constitution for India. They ruled India according to the acts made by the British
Parliament. Among them, Government of India Act - 1935 was an important Act. It was
provided for the establishment of an all-India federation consisting of Provinces and Princely
states. The act divided the powers between the Centre and States in the terms of three lists.
This act introduced diarchy at the Centre. It also introduced the autonomy of the states.

Browse the internet or go through the library books and prepare a chart about other
acts made by the British parliament to rule India. (If necessary, take the help of your
teacher).

9.1.1.Activities related to the Constitution during British
rule :
In the year 1928, a committee was constituted by
all the parties including Indian National Congress to draft
the constitution for India. Motilal Nehru (father of
Jawaharlal Nehru) acted as the chairman of this
committee. This committee submitted its report in the
year 1929. It was known as Nehru report. It was
considered as the first Constitutional Document. But it
could not come into force because the British did not
accept it.
In 1931, the Indian National Congress (INC) at
Karachi session passed a resolution on how Independent
India’s Constitution should look like. Both Nehru report
and Karachi resolution were committed to the Universal
Adult Franchise, Right to Freedom and Equality.

show the nature of the
country, form of the
government, rights and duties
of the citizens is called the
Constitution.
It is either in written
form or non-written form.

form.

9.1.2. The Constituent Assembly :
The Constitution was drafted by an
assembly of elected representatives called the
Constituent Assembly.
First time in 1934, the Indian National
Congress made a demand for a Constituent
Assembly. According to the Cabinet Mission
plan 1946, election to the Constituent
Assembly was held in July 1946.

The Cabinet Mission came to India in
1946 aiming to discuss the transfer of
powers from the British government to
the Indian leadership, with the aim of
preserving India’s unity and granting its
independence. And also, recommended
forming a constituent assembly. The
mission had lord Pethick Lawrence, Sir
Stafford Cripps, and A.V. Alexander as
its members.

The members of the Constituent Assembly were elected
indirectly by the members of the provincial assemblies.
The Cabinet Mission plan allotted seats to each Province
and each Princely State or a group of states.
Accordingly, Provinces or areas under the
British rule elected 292 members and all Princely States
together nominated 93 members. Four members were
elected from Delhi, Ajmer-Mewad, Koorg and British
Baluchistan. With this the total members of the Indian
Constituent Assembly reached 389. Among the 389
members, 26 members were from Scheduled Castes
and 15 members were from women. With the partition
of the country in August 1947, the Constituent
Assembly was also bifurcated into the Indian
Constituent assembly and the Pakistan Constituent
Assembly. The Indian Constituent Assembly had 299
members. It elected Dr. Babu Rajendra Prasad, as its
President and the Pakistan Constituent Assembly
elected Muhammad Ali Jinnah as its President.

Dr. Babu Rajendra Prasad

He was the President of
the Indian Constituent Assembly.
Later, he was elected as the first
President of Independent India
on 24th January 1950, in the last
session of the Constituent
Assembly. He is the only
president to have been re-elected
for a second term (1950 - 1962).

9.1.3. Drafting Committee :
The "Drafting Committee" was entrusted with the responsibility to prepare the
Draft constitution. It was set up on 29th August, 1947 under the chairmanship of Dr. B.R
Ambedkar with seven members. Draft constitution was prepared and submitted to the
Constituent Assembly in 1948. It contained 315 Articles and 8 Schedules.
The Draft Constitution was kept before the public for eight months. During this
long-period critics and advisers had more than sufficient time to express their reaction to
the provisions contained in it. After modifications, the Constitution with 395 Articles, 22
Parts and 8 Schedules was finally adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26th November,
1949 and it came into force on 26th January 1950.

Father of Indian Constitution
Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar, popularly known as
Babasaheb Ambedkar, was a jurist, social activist and a politician.
Bhimrao Ambedkar was born to Bhimabai and Ramji on 14th
April 1891 in Mhow Army Cantonment in Central Provinces
(Madhya Pradesh). Ambedkar’s father was a Subedar in the British
Indian Army and after his retirement in 1894, the family moved

Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
to Satara, of Central Provinces. He faced a number of challenges in his formative years,
which shaped his writings and philosophies. He is regarded as "Father of the Indian
Constitution." He was responsible for the preparation of the draft constitution for
independent India. He was appointed as the First Law Minister of India in 1947. For most
of his life, Ambedkar worked outside the mainstream of politics. He worked for the
welfare of the depressed and poor.

Why do we celebrate Republic

Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas) is celebrated
in India on 26 th November every year to
commemorate the adoption of the Constitution
of India on 26 th November 1949 by the
Constituent Assembly.
The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11
months and 18 days for the preparation of
our Constitution.

stands. It is the basic structure of our Constitution.

How does the State government form and work?
In India we have the government at two levels. One is at the centre and the other
is at the state. The power is divided between two sets of governments one at the central
in Delhi and separate government for each state at state level this is called federal system.
All the states and few union territories have separate governments to run their own
administration and they work according to the Indian constitution. They make laws and
implement them in their state. A government has three main functions - to make the
laws, to execute the laws and to ensure justice for all the people.
Learn more about the federal system, with the help of your teacher.

The State Government is responsible for the administration of the State. The State
Government carried out administration with the help of three organs, 1. Legislature,
2. Executive, 3. Judiciary. Now let us learn more about Legislature, the first one of the three
organs.
10.1. Legislature:
The Governor, Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council are together called a
state legislature. The primary function of the state legislature is to enact Laws.
10.1.1. Governor:
Every state in India have a Governor. The President of India nominates the Governor
on the recommendation of the Prime Minister and his cabinet, for a term of five years.
However sometimes two or three states can have a single Governor. According to article
158(3a) the same person can be appointed as a Governor for two or more States.

Functions of the Governor:
Invites the leader of the majority party to form the Government.
Administers the oath of loyalty to the constitution and secrecy.
Summons the sessions of legislative houses and also announces their prorogue.
Appoints the Judges of all the courts that work under the High Court.
Informs the President about the functioning of the State Government.

10.1.2. Legislative Assembly:
The State Legislative Assembly is a legislative body. Legislative Assembly is the lower
house where all the Members of Legislative Assembly (MLA) meet to discuss on various
issues related to progress and the welfare of the State. Each state is divided into Assembly
constituencies, based on the population of the State.
Elections to the Legislative Assembly:
In general, elections to the state Legislative Assembly are held once in every five
years. The Election Commission announces notification for election in all assembly
constituencies. The individuals, candidates from political parties will contest in elections
with their manifesto. A public declaration of policy and aims especially that announced
before an election by a political party or candidate is called manifesto.

Constituencies. All voters over the age of 18 years and above will vote in that constituency
on election day. The voter ID cards have to be shown to the concerned officer. As part of

completion of polling, all votes are counted on a scheduled date. After counting votes, the
candidate who get the majority of the votes is declared as MLA (Member of Legislative
Assembly) of that constituency.

In such a way the state Government is formed.

Legislative Council. In a bicameral system, (Legislature
divided into two houses) the Legislative Council functions
with the members elected in an indirect election. For every

The Legislative Council has Legislative, Financial, Administrative, and discretionary
powers etc., like the Legislative Assembly. But Legislative Assembly has more economic or
financial powers.

10.1.4. Law making Process (Enact Laws) :
Who makes the Laws? We need laws for the smooth functioning of the systems
in the state. Laws help the state and country to develop and achieve progress. Laws are
enacted by the Legislature. The state government is responsible for the administration of
a particular state. The functions and powers of the state and central Government are
divided into three lists: 1. The Union List 2. The State List 3. The Concurrent List. The
State Government can make laws on the items from state list and concurrent list. Let us
discuss how the bill becomes an Act.

Generally, a member from the ruling party introduces the bill in the State Assembly
or the State Council. Financial bills should be introduced in the Legislative Assembly with
prior approval of the Governor. Copies of a bill will be distributed to the members of the
House.
After the detailed discussions and debate, if required, after some modifications,
voting will be taken up. After the approval of the house by the majority of the members
at the time of voting, the bill will be sent to the next house. The same procedure will
continue to approve the bill in the next house. After that, once it is approved in both the
houses, the bill will be sent to the Governor for his assent. It becomes an Act only when
the Governor accords his approval. Now the Act will be notified in the Gazette. The Gazette
will be sent to the Executive for its enforcement.

Who enforces the laws? The state Executive comprises the Governor, the Chief

The head of the state is the Governor. He/She is appointed by the central government
to ensure that the state government works within the rules and regulations of the
constitution. Find out the name of the Governor of your state?
10.2.2. Chief Minister:
After the elections, the MLAs belonging to the ruling party will elect their leader
who will become the Chief Minister. The Chief Minister then selects ministers from
MLA's. The Governor of the state appoints the Chief Minister and other ministers.
Functions and powers of the chief ministers.
1. He prepares the list of the ministers and send it to the Governor.
2. He allocates portfolios to the ministers.
3. He calls for the cabinet meetings and presides over them.
4. He has the power to co-ordinate and supervise the working of all the departments.

Why the Chief Minister is called real head of the Government? Discuss in class and

According to Article 163(1), there shall be Council of Ministers with the CM as the
head to aid and advise the Governor in the exercise of his functions.
10.2.3 Council of Ministers :
The Chief Minister allocates various ministries to the members of the Cabinet.
The Minister directs the policy of the departments under his/her charge. These policies are
implemented according to the rules by officials of the departments. The Ministries are
responsible for preparing policies and plans which are submitted to the Assembly, for approval.
After the approval by the Assembly, those will be implemented by the executive body. The
cabinet control the financial policy and decides the tax structure for the public welfare of
the state.

10.3. Judiciary - High Court:
Judiciary is one of the three organs of the state government. It is the system of
courts that interprets, defends the law in the name of the state.
The High court is the highest Judicial organ at the State level. As a part of the
independent Judiciary, it functions under the Apex court of the country, the Supreme
Court. The State High court consists of a Chief Justice and other Judges. The number of
judges in the High Court is not the same in all states.

The President of India appoints the Chief Justice and he can hold the office until
he/she completes the age of 62 years. Apart from the High Court at state level, there are
tribunals, and District Courts at lower levels. The Judiciary ensure Justice to the people
without any bias. Lok Adalats (People’s Court) are also established by the Government of
India to settle dispute through conciliation and compromise.
You have learned in this lesson that the bill is introduced in the house and after
being approved by the house it is sent to the governor and after the governor assent the
bill becomes law and is published in the gazette. This state government gazette is sent to
officials. To enforce laws the cabinet enlists the help of government officials such as the
district collector. Let us now learn about district level administration.
10.4. District level Administration :
What we need to know in the district administration is about the district collector
and the department of justice in the district. Each district in India has an officer-in-charge
who represents the state government in that area in the capacity as district Collector, or
District Magistrate.
10.4.1. The District Collector :
The District Collector is the head of the district administration and is recruited
through Union Public Service Commission and allotted to states, by the Central Government.
He has to take responsibility of various departments like Revenue (all matters connected
to land records and Revenue Administration), law & order (to maintain Law and Order
to maintain Social harmony), local self-government, agriculture, disaster management (to
take immediate actions at the time of disasters and prevent or minimize the damage) and
Election duties (to conduct elections) etc. Let us discuss about the officials who help the
district collector in looking after administration in district.

Superintendent of Police : There will be a Superintendent of Police in every district
headquarter. He is the chief Police officer of the district. He helps the District Collector in
maintaining law and order in the District.
Revenue Divisional Officer : The responsibility of the Revenue Divisional officer, is to
maintain law and order in Sub-Division, to collect land revenue, to conduct free and fair
elections at Division level. Land acquisition and rehabilitation and other duties entrusted
by the District Collector.
Tahsildar : He is the Chief administrative and executive head of the department at Mandal
Level. He is responsible for the proper assessment and prompt collection of revenues and
maintenance of land records.
Village Revenue Officer : Maintenance of village revenue records and revenue accounts
promptly and accurately. Collection of land revenue, Taxes and other sums (a particular
amout of money) pertaining to revenue department in village level administration, which
includes inspection of survey stones, issue of certificates like nativity and residence certificates
etc.,
10.4.2. District level Judiciary :
The district Judiciary Department consists of district and divisional courts. Division
courts administer justice at the divisional level and district court at the district level.

District Court: The Court at the district level is known as the District Court. The district
court has a Chief District Judge and some other Judges. The main function is prosecute and
finalize various cases in the district level. The judgement of Divisional Court may be
appealed in the District Court.

disputes/cases pending in the court of law or at pre-litigation stage are settled/compromised
amicably. Lok Adalats have been given statutory status under the Legal Service Authorities
Act 1987. Civil cases, matrimonial cases, and petty offence cases are mainly referred to Lok
Adalat.

3. Judiciary. Department of legislature can enact laws. Executive body enforce the laws.
Judiciary body interpret the laws. Thus the state government administers the state and

Consumer :
A Consumer is a person who purchases a product or avails a service for a
consideration, either for his personal use or to earn his livelihood by means of selfemployment.

Consumer Protection :
Protecting consumer rights is a very important aspect of the market. Consumer
protection is a group of laws enacted to protect rights of consumer, fair trade, competition
and accurate information in the market place.
Consumer protection Act 2019 :
On 9th August 2019 consumer protection act was approved. It aims to provide timely
and effective administration and settlement of consumer dispute in the digital age.
This Act has broadened the concept of Consumerism. It defines consumer as any
person who buys any goods, whether through offline or online transactions, electronic
means, teleshopping, direct selling or multi-level marketing.
Consumer Rights :
1. The right to be protected against the marketing of goods, products or services which
are hazardous to life and property.
2. The right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and

price of goods, products or services, as the case may be, so as to protect the consumer
against unfair trade practices.
The right to be assured, wherever possible, access to a variety of goods, products or
services at competitive prices.
The right to be heard and to be assured that consumers interests will receive due
consideration at appropriate fora.
The right to seek redressal against unfair trade practices or restrictive trade practices
or unscrupulous exploitation of consumers.
The right to consumer awareness.

officer in India. In October 2019, she took over
as Sub Collector in Thiruvananthapuram,
Kerala. Pranjal Patil pursued her dreams despite
her blindness from a very young age. She was
not afraid of her miserable condition. Weakness
has her desire to serve the country resulted in
clearing civil services exams conducted by UPSC in 2017. She was ranked 124th and
proved that she can overcome all obstacles through willpower and hardwork.

Seema Rao
Seema Rao has achieved what no other
Indian woman has done so far. She is the
country’s first woman commando trainer. In
partnership with her husband, Major Deepak
Rao, she has trained over 15,000 soldiers in
close-quarter battles. Also qualified as a
professional medical doctor, she possesses an
MBA in crisis management. To top it all, she
is one of only 10 women in the world who are trained in Jeet Kune Do - a form of martial
arts developed by Bruce Lee.

Rajkumari Devi
Rajkumari Devi, a farmer from Bihar,
rode a bicycle in many villages and shared her
experiences on kitchen farming with a rural
woman who instilled a sense of
entrepreneurship. Her goal is to show how
women can become financially independent
through agriculture and small businesses. To this
end, Rajkumari has started a non-profit center
called Anandpur Jyothi, which collects fresh produce from various SHG-driven farms and
takes it to a group of women who use it to make processed products such as jellies, jams
and pickles. She was honored with the Padma Shri award in 2019 for her services.

Vandana Shiva
Vandana Shiva is an environmentalist and
environmental rights activist, and founder of the Research
Foundation for Science, Technology and Ecology. It's an
independent research organization that conducts research
on environmental and social issues. Vandana’s efforts led
to the formation of a national movement called
Navadhanya to protect the diversity and integrity of living
resources, especially indigenous seeds. She received the
Right Livelihood Award in 1993 and the Sydney Peace
Prize in 2010.

Laxmi Agarwal
Laxmi Agarwal is an acid attack survivor.
She fights for the rights of acid attack victims.
She was attacked with acid in 2005, at age 15,
by a 32-year-old man. Her petition led the
Supreme Court to order the central and state
governments to regulate the sale of acid, and the
Parliament to make prosecutions of acid attacks
easier to pursue. She is the director of Chhanv
Foundation, an NGO dedicated to helping the survivors of acid attacks in India. Laxmi
received a 2014 International Women of Courage award by US First Lady Michelle Obama.
She was also chosen as the NDTV Indian of the Year.

Addala Suryakala
Addala Suryakala is from Srikakulam district.
Her husband fell ill and it was difficult to manage home.
Even the rent of the house could not be paid. With the
help of NABARD she learned modern techniques in
the manufacture of bronze and brassware, and became
proficient in engraving on lightweight modern utensils.
It has been able to expand its business nationally and
internationally, providing employment to many. She was
an ideal for many women with her perseverance, hard
work, and philosophy of changing over time.

Nandini Harinath
Nandini Harinath is a rocket scientist at
the ISRO (Indian Space Research Organization)
Satellite Center in Bangalore. Nandini has been
with ISRO for the last 20 years. She has served
on the Mars Orbiter Mission Mangalayan,
Project Manager, Mission Designer and Deputy
Director of Operations. She has served in 14
missions at ISRO for 20 years.

Archana Soreng
Archana Soreng, a tribal girl from Odisha.
She holds a degree in Political Science from Patna
Women’s College and a Master's Degree from
the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Mumbai.
She later joined an NGO called ‘Vasundhara’ in
Odisha and organized awareness programs on
forests and environmental protection. Her
articles on tribal traditions, the measures they
take to protect the environment, and the difficulties involved have been published on
national and international websites. As a result, she has been selected by as one of the
seven members of the Youth Advisory group on climate change to provide solutions to the
climate crisis and rendering her services internationally.
